lesson.title: When More Comes with Less: Negative Association in Depth
lesson.summary: Explore negative association in depth using a car depreciation example and a heating bill example, and learn why a negative pattern still requires the same causal caution as a positive one.
lesson.body:
A negative association is the mirror image of positive association: it describes the case where the response variable tends to decrease as the explanatory variable increases. Tracing a scatterplot with a negative association from left to right shows the point cloud drifting downward, even though individual points may bounce a little above or below the overall downward trend.

Return to the car example: five cars aged 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 years have resale values of about 22,000, 19,000, 17,000, 14,000, and 11,000 dollars. As age increases by one year at a time, resale value consistently drops, roughly 3,000 dollars at each step. Tracing those points from left to right shows a clear downward drift, the defining feature of a negative association. Depreciation is a familiar, everyday negative association: the older the car, the lower its market value tends to be.

Negative associations are just as common as positive ones once you start looking for them. The relationship between average monthly temperature and a household's heating bill is a good example: in a colder month, furnaces run longer and the bill climbs, in a warmer month, the furnace runs less and the bill falls. As temperature increases across the months of a year, heating cost tends to decrease, which is a negative association between two everyday quantitative variables that almost anyone can verify by looking at their own utility bills.

As with positive association, a negative association describes what the data shows, not why it happens, and the two are easy to conflate. Some negative associations come from a genuine causal mechanism, like colder weather directly causing higher furnace use. Others arise more subtly. A person's hours spent on homework and hours spent watching television in a single day, for instance, are often negatively associated largely because both are competing for the same fixed 24 hours, not because homework somehow prevents television from existing. Before assuming a negative association reflects one variable driving down the other, consider whether there is a simpler structural or lurking explanation.

Numerically, when a linear relationship is negative, the correlation coefficient r you will compute soon comes out negative, somewhere between -1 and 0, with values closer to -1 describing a tighter, more consistent downward pattern. The sign of r is nothing more than a numerical restatement of the direction you can already see by eye on a well-drawn scatterplot.

Getting the direction right, positive or negative, is not a minor detail. Reversing the sign of an association in a written conclusion completely flips its meaning, turning the claim that studying more raises your score into the claim that studying more lowers your score. Always state direction as the first, and most basic, description of any relationship you see in a scatterplot before moving on to describe its form and strength.
